267.title: Where have you hidden (Spiritual Canticle)
267.hook: the soul searches the woods and fields asking where the beloved went
267.howItsDone: Carmelites and many Catholics pray with John's Spiritual Canticle and his commentary on it, and the Church reads the Song of Songs as a love song between God and the soul, and between Christ and the Church.

segments.voice: Yesterday, faith as a dark light, a cloud that lights the night. Your line was walk by faith. What one step did you take? Today, we open the love poem John began in his prison cell. Day two hundred sixty-seven.

You wake up, and the other side of the bed is empty. Still warm. They were just here. You call their name. Nothing. You check the kitchen, the porch, the yard. You start asking anyone you see: have you seen them? Which way did they go? That's how John of the Cross opens his longest poem, the Spiritual Canticle. Not with an answer. With a question, half a cry, from someone who was loved and then found herself alone. Today's word is that question.
screen: `THE OTHER SIDE OF THE BED.` → `STILL WARM.` → `HAVE YOU SEEN THEM?`

segments.voice: First, the cry. The poem's first line, in John's Spanish: "¿Adónde te escondiste, Amado, y me dejaste con gemido?" Where have you hidden, Beloved, and left me moaning? The bride is the soul. The Beloved is God, and for John, Christ. He's modeling it on the Song of Songs, where the bride says, in the Douay-Rheims: "In my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loveth: I sought him, and found him not." Second, the search. The bride doesn't sit and wait. She goes out. She asks the shepherds on the hills. She crosses mountains and riverbanks. Then she turns to the woods and thickets themselves, planted by the Beloved's hand, and asks them: has he passed by here? Third, the answer. And the creation answers her. In John's Spanish, the woods say he passed through these groves in haste, pouring out a thousand graces, and just by looking at them as he went, "vestidos los dejó de hermosura," he left them clothed in beauty. The world is lovely, the poem says, because God glanced at it on his way through. Fourth, not enough. But here's the ache. The bride isn't satisfied with the trees. They're beautiful, but they're traces, messengers. She wants him. John says this is what happens as love grows: the world's beauty points to God, and makes you want God more, not less. Nature isn't a substitute. It's a trail of footprints. And the poem keeps going, for dozens of stanzas, until the bride finds the Beloved.
screen: `WHERE HAVE YOU HIDDEN, BELOVED?` · `SHE ASKS THE WOODS AND HILLS.` · `HE LEFT THEM CLOTHED IN BEAUTY.` · `FOOTPRINTS, NOT THE BELOVED.` · then, large: `¿ADÓNDE TE ESCONDISTE, AMADO?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for God outdoors. If you can, step outside, or to a window. Find one living thing: a tree, a patch of sky, a weed in a crack, a bird. Look at it slowly, as if someone you love had just walked past it. If you pray, you can ask it John's question, where have you hidden, and listen. If you don't, just let the beauty of the thing be a trace of something larger. The bell holds the time.
Where have you hidden. The first cry of John's Spiritual Canticle: the soul searching the woods and fields for her Beloved, who left them clothed in beauty. Today's word.
Your line: where have you hidden. Today, on the way somewhere, look for one thing that seems clothed in beauty, and let it point you further. Day two hundred sixty-seven.

268.title: The log in the fire (Dark Night 2.10)
268.hook: wet wood hisses and blackens before it becomes flame
268.howItsDone: Catholic spiritual directors use John's image of the log in the fire to reassure people who feel more aware of their faults as they grow in prayer, and his Living Flame of Love is read as the fulfillment of that image.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Spiritual Canticle: where have you hidden, and woods clothed in beauty. Your line was where have you hidden. What did you find outdoors? Today, John's most down-to-earth picture of the night. Day two hundred sixty-eight.

If you've ever built a campfire with damp wood, you know what happens. You wait for a big, cheerful flame. Instead you get hissing. Popping. Water bubbling out of the ends of the log. Clouds of gray smoke in your eyes. The bark goes black and ugly. It smells bad. It looks like the fire is ruining the wood, and you start to wonder if it'll ever catch. And then, slowly, it does. John of the Cross knew fires like that. Today's word is his picture.
screen: `A CAMPFIRE WITH DAMP WOOD.` → `HISSING, SMOKE, BLACKENED BARK.` → `THEN, SLOWLY, IT CATCHES.`

segments.voice: First, the stages. In the Dark Night, book two, chapter ten, John walks through it. When fire first touches a log, it doesn't set it ablaze. It starts by drying it, driving out the dampness, so the wood seems to weep. Then it blackens it, makes it dark and ugly, even gives off a bad smell. Only as it dries does the fire give it heat and light. And at the end, the wood becomes fire itself, as bright and hot as the flame. Second, the log is the soul. The fire is God's love. When that love first gets close, John says, the soul doesn't feel lit up. It feels worse. It suddenly sees its own damp and dark places, faults it didn't know it had. Third, the surprise. Here's John's key point. The fire isn't making the wood ugly. The ugliness was already in the wood. The fire is just drawing it out, so it can be burned away. So when someone who's trying to love God suddenly feels more aware of their failings, John says, that's often not a sign of getting worse. It's the smoke. It means the fire is working. Fourth, the flame. And the same fire that hurt at first becomes the one that delights. The log doesn't stay a log with a fire next to it. It becomes flame. John wrote a whole other poem about that end, the Living Flame of Love. So be patient with the smoke. Yours, and other people's.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be patient with your own smoke. Settle and breathe. Think of one fault you've been noticing in yourself lately, maybe more than before. Impatience, envy, a sharp tongue. Instead of beating yourself up, picture it as smoke rising off a log, damp coming out so it can burn clean. If you pray, you can let God's love keep working on it. If you don't, try just being gentle with yourself, the way you'd wait out a smoky fire. The bell holds the time.
The log in the fire. John's picture of the dark night: God's love first dries and blackens the soul, drawing out what's there, before it turns it into flame. Today's word.

269.title: In the evening, love (Sayings of Light and Love)
269.hook: at the end we will be judged on love
269.howItsDone: Catholics often quote John's saying on the evening of life, which the Catechism cites in its teaching on judgment, and many make an evening examen asking how they loved that day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the log in the fire: first it hisses and blackens, then it becomes flame. Your line was first smoke, then flame. Whose smoke were you patient with? Today, one sentence John left behind. Day two hundred sixty-nine.

Imagine the final exam of your life. What's on it? Most of us, if we're honest, picture something like a report card. How much did you get done. How much did you earn. Did you keep the rules. How many people know your name. Maybe a section on religion: did you pray enough, go to church enough, believe the right things. John of the Cross wrote down what he thought would be on that exam. It's one line, from a small collection of his sayings, and it's short enough to fit on your palm. Today's word is how it begins.
screen: `THE FINAL EXAM OF YOUR LIFE.` → `A REPORT CARD?` → `ONE LINE ON A PALM.`

segments.voice: First, the sayings. John wrote short, sharp sayings on slips of paper for the friars and nuns he guided. They were gathered later and are known as the Sayings of Light and Love. Some are a single sentence. Second, the line. In John's Spanish: "A la tarde te examinarán en el amor." In the evening, you will be examined in love. The evening is the end of life. The exam has one subject. Not how much you knew about prayer. Not how many dark nights you understood. Love. The Catechism of the Catholic Church quotes this line when it teaches about judgment. Third, where he got it. It's not John's invention. It comes straight from Jesus's picture of the last judgment in Matthew's Gospel, where the nations are sorted by whether they fed the hungry, welcomed the stranger, visited the sick and the prisoner. And the king says, in the Douay-Rheims: "as long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me." Think back to John's own life: the boy washing the sick in the hospital, the prisoner in the dark room. He knew this passage from both sides. Fourth, what to do about it. Near the end of his life, John wrote a letter to a nun who was upset about how someone had treated her. His advice has been repeated ever since. Where there is no love, put love, and you will draw out love. Not wait for it. Put it there. Everything we've learned about nights and fire and nada comes back to this. The whole point was love.
screen: `SAYINGS ON SLIPS OF PAPER.` · `EXAMINED IN LOVE.` · `THE LEAST OF THESE.` · `WHERE THERE IS NO LOVE, PUT LOVE.` · then, large: `A LA TARDE TE EXAMINARÁN EN EL AMOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask what love needs today. Settle and breathe. Picture this evening, the end of today. Imagine looking back on it. Now ask: what would love have done today? Let one face come to mind. Someone hungry, lonely, sick, difficult, or simply waiting to hear from you. What's one thing love needs you to do for them? If you pray, you can ask God to show you. If you don't, trust the first honest answer. The bell holds the time.
In the evening. The start of John's saying: in the evening of life, you will be examined in love. Today's word.
Your line: judged on love. Today, find the place where there's no love, and put some there. Then, this evening, notice what it drew out. Day two hundred sixty-nine.

270.title: Úbeda, 1591
270.hook: dying, he asked to hear the Song of Songs, not the prayers for the dying
270.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint John of the Cross on December 14, the day he died in Úbeda, and the Church's prayers for the dying are still read at deathbeds, sometimes alongside readings a person has asked for.

segments.voice: Yesterday, in the evening of life, we will be examined in love. Your line was judged on love. Where did you put love today? Today, John's own evening comes. Day two hundred seventy.

By 1591, John of the Cross has lost almost everything the world counts. He's forty-nine. The leaders of the reform he helped start have turned against him in a quarrel over how it should be run. He's been stripped of every office and sent to a remote friary in the south. Then he gets sick: a fever, and an infection in his leg that won't heal. He needs a town with doctors. The story goes that he could have gone to a friary where he was loved, and chose Úbeda, where he wasn't known. The prior there doesn't like him. Today's word is that town.
screen: `STRIPPED OF EVERY OFFICE.` → `A FEVER, AN INFECTED LEG.` → `A PRIOR WHO DOESN'T LIKE HIM.`

segments.voice: First, the prior. The man in charge at Úbeda resented John, and for weeks he treated him coldly. He complained about the cost of his care, and gave him one of the poorest cells. John didn't fight back. The story told about the prior is that he later wept and changed his mind about John. Second, the sores. The infection spread. The doctors cut into his leg again and again, without anything we'd call a painkiller. The friars who nursed him remembered that he hardly complained, and thanked everyone who helped him. Third, the last night. On December 13, he kept asking what time it was. When they told him it was almost midnight, the story goes, he said he would soon go to sing the morning prayers in heaven. The friars began to read the prayers for the dying, the ones the Church has used for centuries. And John stopped them, gently. He asked instead for the Song of Songs, the love poetry of the Bible. They read it to him. And he said, what precious pearls. Fourth, the song. Picture which lines they might have read. In the Douay-Rheims: "Arise, make haste, my love, my dove, my beautiful one, and come. For winter is now past, the rain is over and gone." A man who'd written so much about dark nights, dying in a cold cell, asking to hear about spring. He died just after midnight, on December 14, 1591. The Church keeps his feast on that day. For him, it seems, death wasn't a final night. It was the Beloved saying: arise, and come.
screen: `A PRIOR WHO RESENTED HIM.` · `SORES, AND NO COMPLAINT.` · `NOT THOSE PRAYERS. THE SONG.` · `WINTER IS NOW PAST.` · then, large: `ARISE, MAKE HASTE, MY LOVE, AND COME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read Song of Songs 2:10 to 13. If you have a Bible nearby, find it. If not, listen to these words once more: Arise, make haste, my love, my dove, my beautiful one, and come. For winter is now past, the rain is over and gone. Sit with them. Think of a winter in your own life that's ending, or that you hope will end. If you pray, you can hear these words as God's to you. If you don't, let them be about spring. The bell holds the time.

271.title: A doctor for the dark
271.hook: named a Doctor of the Church in 1926; a guide for anyone in the night
271.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of St. John of the Cross on December 14, and spiritual directors often point people in long seasons of dryness to his Dark Night and Ascent of Mount Carmel.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Úbeda, 1591. Dying, John asked to hear the Song of Songs, not the prayers for the dying. Your line was arise and come. Did you read those verses slowly? Today we close our weeks with the small friar. Day two hundred seventy-one.

Think of someone you know who is in a long, dark stretch. A diagnosis. A grief that won't lift. A prayer life that has gone flat and silent for months. People in that place often say the same thing: I thought I was doing it wrong. For a long time there was no handbook for that feeling. Then a small friar, jailed by his own brothers, wrote one, in poems and commentaries. And three and a half centuries after he died, the Church gave him a title it keeps for its greatest teachers. Today: a doctor for the dark.
screen: `A LONG, DARK STRETCH.` → `I THOUGHT I WAS DOING IT WRONG.` → `A DOCTOR FOR THE DARK.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Doctor comes from the Latin docere, to teach. A Doctor of the Church isn't a physician. It's a teacher the whole Church is told it can trust. The title asks for three things: a holy life, deep learning, and a pope's declaration. It's rare. The first four were named in 1298: Ambrose, Augustine, Jerome and Gregory the Great. Even now there are fewer than forty. Second, the long road. John died in 1591, mistrusted by some of his own superiors. He was beatified in 1675 and canonized a saint in 1726. Then, in 1926, Pope Pius XI named him a Doctor of the Church. He's often called the Mystical Doctor. Third, what he teaches. Look back over these weeks. The dark night: when prayer goes dry, God may not be gone. Dry is not gone. The three signs: the longing stays. Nada: nothing, then everything. The bird on a thread. The log that smokes before it catches. Put it together and his teaching fits in one surprising sentence: the dark can be part of the road, not the end of it. Fourth, why it matters on an ordinary Tuesday. John is careful. In the Dark Night he says some dryness comes from melancholy or bad health, and that isn't the night he means. He never makes pain holy for its own sake. What he gives people in the dark is company, and a map. Someone has been here. Someone wrote down the way through. Paul said it long before him, in the Douay-Rheims: "For we walk by faith, and not by sight." The Mystical Doctor spent his life on that line.
screen: `DOCERE — TO TEACH.` · `CANONIZED 1726, DOCTOR 1926.` · `THE DARK CAN BE PART OF THE ROAD.` · `COMPANY, AND A MAP.` · then, large: `WE WALK BY FAITH, AND NOT BY SIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bring someone to mind. Settle, and breathe. Think of one person who is in a dark stretch right now. Don't fix it. Just hold their face for a moment. Then ask one question: would it help them to know someone has walked this road before? If it would, later today you might send them his name, or one line from these weeks: dry is not gone. Only if it feels kind, not like a lecture. If you pray, you can hold them in the quiet. The bell holds the time.
Doctor of the Church. A teacher the whole Church can trust, from the Latin for teach. John of the Cross has held the title since 1926. Today's word.

Your line: the night is a way. Today, when something feels dark, try saying it once: a way, not a wall. That closes our eighteen days with the small friar. Tomorrow, a new guide. Day two hundred seventy-one.

272.title: A restless young man (1915)
272.hook: born in France, orphaned young, drifting through Cambridge and Columbia
272.howItsDone: Many Catholics read Thomas Merton's autobiography as a modern story of conversion, and Augustine's line about the restless heart is often quoted in Catholic preaching and in the Catechism itself.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Doctor of the Church for the dark: John of the Cross. Your line was the night is a way. Did you think of someone walking through one? Today, a new guide, and a very different life. Day two hundred seventy-two.

Rome, 1933. An eighteen-year-old is wandering the city on his own. Both his parents are dead. He has money from a guardian, a head full of novels, and no plan at all. He goes into the old churches, not to pray, but to look at the mosaics, because he likes art. And standing in front of those gold and blue walls, something catches in him that he can't name. He'll spend years running from it. His name is Thomas Merton. He'll become the most famous monk in America. For the next eighteen days, he's our guide. Today: a restless young man.
screen: `ROME, 1933. EIGHTEEN, AND ALONE.` → `INTO THE CHURCHES FOR THE ART.` → `A RESTLESS YOUNG MAN.`

segments.voice: First, the losses. Merton was born on January 31, 1915, in Prades, a small town in the south of France. His father was a painter from New Zealand, his mother an American artist. When he was six, his mother died of cancer. When he was fifteen, his father died too. After that he was moved around: schools in France and England, holidays with relatives, a guardian in London. A boy with a suitcase, never quite at home anywhere. Second, the drifting. At Cambridge he drank, stayed out, failed at being careful, and left after a year he later looked back on with real shame. His guardian sent him to America. At Columbia University in New York he was clever, funny, restless. He wrote for the humor magazine, loved jazz, and flirted with politics. He was busy all the time and happy almost never. Third, the mosaics. Something from Rome stayed with him. In those churches he'd looked at pictures of Christ, and for the first time he wanted to know who that was. He didn't act on it yet. He just couldn't forget it. Fourth, why restless is a start. Long before Merton, Augustine wrote at the opening of his Confessions that the human heart is restless until it rests in God. Catholics have loved that sentence for sixteen hundred years. It doesn't treat restlessness as a failure. It treats it as a sign that you're made for something you haven't found yet. Merton's early life looks like a mess. Read with Augustine, it looks like a search.
screen: `BORN IN FRANCE, ORPHANED YOUNG.` · `DRIFTING: CAMBRIDGE, THEN COLUMBIA.` · `THE MOSAICS HE COULDN'T FORGET.` · `RESTLESS UNTIL IT RESTS IN GOD.` · then, large: `A SEARCH, NOT A MESS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with your own restlessness. Get still, and notice what doesn't want to be still. The itch to check your phone. A thought that keeps circling. A sense that something's missing. Don't fix it and don't scold it. Just find where it lives in your body, your chest, your hands, your jaw, and let it be there. Then ask it, gently: what are you looking for? You don't need an answer. If you pray, you can offer the restlessness itself. The bell holds the time.
A restless young man. Thomas Merton at eighteen: orphaned, gifted, drifting, and carrying one picture from Rome he couldn't shake. Today's word.
Your line: restless is a start. Today, when you feel that itch for something more, don't just scroll past it. Notice it, and let it count as a beginning. Day two hundred seventy-two.

273.title: A convert in New York (1938)
273.hook: he reads philosophy, walks into a church, and is baptized
273.howItsDone: Adults who become Catholic today usually walk a path of study and prayer called the Order of Christian Initiation of Adults, and are often baptized or received into the Church at the Easter Vigil.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a restless young man: Merton, orphaned, drifting through Cambridge and Columbia. Your line was restless is a start. Where did your restlessness show up? Today it starts to go somewhere. Day two hundred seventy-three.

New York, 1937. Merton is at Columbia, and he buys a book for a class: a history of medieval philosophy. On the train home he opens it and sees the little Latin stamp inside that says a Catholic censor approved it. He's so annoyed he nearly throws it out the window. He doesn't. He reads it. And one idea in it cracks something open. A year later he's standing in a priest's doorway on a rainy afternoon, saying: I want to become a Catholic. Today: how that happened.
screen: `A BOOK HE NEARLY THREW OUT.` → `ONE IDEA CRACKS IT OPEN.` → `I WANT TO BECOME A CATHOLIC.`

segments.voice: First, the idea. The book was Étienne Gilson's The Spirit of Medieval Philosophy. Merton had assumed God was a vague, fuzzy feeling. Gilson showed him the medieval idea that God is not one more thing in the universe, but being itself, the reason anything exists at all. Merton later wrote that this gave him a whole new respect for the faith. Second, the friends. A professor named Mark Van Doren, a poet friend named Robert Lax. And a surprise: a Hindu monk visiting New York, called Bramachari, who told him to read Augustine's Confessions and The Imitation of Christ, the great books of his own Western tradition. Merton never forgot that kindness. Third, the church. One Sunday in August 1938 he went, alone, to Mass at Corpus Christi Church near the university. He left before the end, nervous, and walked down the street feeling happier than he'd felt in years. Then, weeks later, he was reading about the poet Gerard Manley Hopkins becoming a Catholic, and he put the book down, walked through the rain to the rectory, and asked. On November 16, 1938, he was baptized. Fourth, the word. Convert comes from the Latin convertere, to turn around. And here's the Catholic twist: the turning isn't only the person's own work. In John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus says: "No man can come to me, except the Father, who hath sent me, draw him." Looking back, Merton saw it the same way. A book, a teacher, a monk, a Mass. Someone was drawing him the whole time.
screen: `GOD AS BEING ITSELF.` · `A TEACHER, A POET, A HINDU MONK.` · `CORPUS CHRISTI, AUGUST 1938.` · `CONVERTERE — TO TURN AROUND.` · then, large: `EXCEPT THE FATHER DRAW HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember what first drew you. Settle and breathe. Go back to the first time faith, or the question of God, caught your attention. Maybe a person. A place. A song, a funeral, a book you almost threw away. It doesn't matter if you're sure of anything now. Just find that first thread and look at it for a moment. Whose hand was in it? If you pray, you can say thank you for it. The bell holds the time.
Convert. From the Latin convertere, to turn around. For Merton, a turning that took years, through a book, some friends, and one quiet Mass. Today's word.

Your line: someone was drawing him. Look back at this week: where have you hidden, the log in the fire, judged on love, arise and come, the night is a way, then a restless young man turning around. Today, notice one thing that's drawing you. Day two hundred seventy-three.

original.note: Latin: to turn around, the root of convert and conversion.

trapdoor: what you thought: a convert is someone who switched teams.
what it means: someone who turned around, slowly, and for Merton the turning came through a book, friends, a monk and a Mass.
what a scholar hears: convertere, to turn around; and John 6:44, the Catholic sense that the turning is drawn by God before it's chosen.
